tldr: Headlines across 12 country buckets report Israeli airstrikes on Syria's Abu al-Duhur airbase through two dominant frames: Israel's security-threat justification (blocking Turkish troop deployment) and a multinational condemnation chorus. A smaller set of headlines foreground US-Netanyahu political friction, while the Straits Times alone leads with the deconfliction diplomacy that followed.

single_outlet_findings.finding: The only headline to name US political frustration with Netanyahu by his nickname ('Bibi'), converting a security event into a US-Israel domestic-political story at the title layer where every other outlet foregrounded the strike or condemnation.

The only headline to characterise Syria's restraint as 'appeasement' — a pejorative framing absent from all other outlets — and to describe the strike as 'warning Ankara' rather than striking a military airbase, uniquely foregrounding an adversarial editorial angle.
The only headline to lead with the US-brokered deconfliction mechanism rather than the strike itself or its condemnation, advertising the diplomatic aftermath as the story before any reader clicks.

bottom_line: At the headline layer this is a dual-frame story — Israel's security rationale and a multinational condemnation chorus — but three outliers reveal divergent editorial priorities: Axios frames it as a US political rupture with Netanyahu, Tehran Times characterises Syria's restraint as 'appeasement', and the Straits Times alone leads with the deconfliction diplomacy rather than the military incident.
